The Q’iq’ewetó:lthel Heritage Facility will protect the remains of highly significant and currently exposed ancestral Sts’ailes-Coast Salish plank houses on the Sts’ailes reserve, Harrison River. The Heritage Facility will help to preserve the heritage plank houses from rain, snow, high water flooding and vandalism. By safeguarding the physical site, it will be possible to continue learning and sharing more about how people lived in this place.

properties.project_brief: The Preserving the Knowledge of Our Elders Project will preserve, digitize and archive Sts’ailes information about our history, culture, ancestors and landscape into a format that is useful to leadership and other community members. This includes building a database for storing our family genealogies. These are invaluable records that connect us to our Elders, ancestors and relations throughout the Salish Sea.

Mentors and apprentices will work together to tan a deer hide. While learning skinning, scraping and smoking techniques, apprentices will also learn Secwepemc words, sentences, stories and protocol. Elders will also share their knowledge and stories about proper care and storage of the tanned hide until it can be used to make moccasins or gloves.

Recording, documenting, digitizing and archiving oral history and traditional protocol and laws from Elders / Knowledge Keepers is vital to securing the information for our future generations. Interviews will be conducted in group settings as well as one-on-one meetings. Some interviews will be conducted on the land with day trips to traditionally significant areas.
This project will conduct a language status assessment survey.
These workshops will blend digital art and storytelling, fostering cultural knowledge and creativity among participants.

The goal of this project is to record interviews with Bonaparte Elders and Knowledge Keepers to identify and document Indigenous heritage, cultural areas, objects, songs, stories and traditions and Indigenous ways of knowing at the McAbee site. This project will provide the path forward for BC Heritage Branch and Bonaparte First Nation to achieve a united vision and commitment to Bonaparte’s cultural heritage practices, expressions and worldviews.

This project will build an active transportation trail that connects our school to the other village of our community. The trail will be a living story through the forest, featuring trail signs that tell stories of our history, families and heritage.

Sulhween Snuw'uy'ulh Elder Stories of Stz'uminus Program is a land-based, inclusive, experiential project where students engage in oral storytelling with Elders out on the land. Elders will be invited to share knowledge from their individual experiences, and students will ask them questions.

The Reclaiming My Language program is based on a successful program that was developed in Norway and Sweden for and by Indigenous Sami people. The model has since been adapted based on the input of First Nations in B.C. The course uses Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) to support Silent Speakers to overcome blockages about using their Indigenous language in their communities. The program will run for 10 weeks, from the last week of September 2023 to the last week of November 2023.

We would like to translate and upload the second vocabulary book of the Paul Creek Curriculum and our cultural calendar. The calendar will have words and phrases associated with the various plants, medicines, foods and cultural activities associated with each season. We will also continue to develop, translate, record and upload the First Nations Language Essentials books.

This project consists of daily immersion classes for adults, development of a language nest, development of a new assessment method for adult language learning and creation of new Hulq'umi'num curriculum resources. Additionally, the community, especially Elders, will be engaged in the development and operation of the language nest, and parents of children in the language nest will be encouraged to join the adult language classes to encourage more language in the home.

This program will provide Tahltan youth with opportunities to learn Tahltan language and traditional cultural activities. Nature walks through local trails will give the chance to identify trees, plants, animals, birds, bugs and weather in our language. Participants will also learn traditional Tahltan medicine identification and harvesting. Finally, participants will create regalia such as moosehide moccasins, button blankets, shawl/vests and canvas-top mukluks.

This project is focused on re-opening the language nest, including everything from staff recruitment and training, community engagement and resource development (handbook, forms, signage, etc.) to securing and setting up a location. Once operational, the language nest will run three days a week.

This project consists of two parts. The first involves building a community-accessible food preparation site based on traditional Takla infrastructure styles, featuring a log cabin with a kitchen, two smokehouses, sheltered gazebos for gatherings and replicas of historical tools that can be used in demonstrations and classes. The second part of the project involves upgrading the Red Rock Trail, an ancient trail used by Takla ancestors for hunting and gathering.

Takla First Nation would like to collect recordings of stories, words and phrases from Elders and Knowledge Keepers. This includes information about traditional land use and land claims, family histories and traditions; deaths and marriages; and stories and experiences.

This program takes Elders and Knowledge Keepers onto the land to talk about plants and their traditional uses along with cultural knowledge such as creation stories, personal histories and more. The tangible result will be a catalogue of plant names and uses translated into traditional languages as well as audio and video recordings to be uploaded on the Takla website and FirstVoices site. Youth will accompany the expeditions so that they can hear from the Elders first hand.
The Knowledge Keeper Gathering will bring together Elders and cultural leaders that have shared history and language with Takla to revitalize and strengthen community ties.
This project will teach youth and children at Atlin School about cultural practices in Tlingit around food, foraging, artwork and other traditions with Elders and Knowledge Keepers.

Haa Kusteeyi (Our Way of Life) is a three-day festival rooted in celebrating our culture and language. Each night, our Elders and Knowledge Keepers will teach community members and visitors about our Tlingit culture and history. We seek funding to organize the events, provide honoraria, conduct professional video and audio recording, and transcribe the histories for later access.

This project will develop an e-book of Tlingit oral histories, stories, protocols and language. This is a multi-pronged project that will provide continued benefits for the community into the future. It lays a foundation for more detailed and nuanced work regarding the management of cultural heritage materials and provides us with the opportunity to fully engage with our culture and history.

The Kwikwetlem Historical Cemetery Revitalization Project includes five development phases, including site development and construction, as well as site management and operations. Our traditional burial grounds adjacent to the Coquitlam River are at risk because of historical changes in the Coquitlam River Watershed. We are working on flood remediation strategies, burial site upgrades and a sustainable plan for long-term operations. Site upgrades will feature high-quality landscaping, fencing and horticultural displays, and a memorial to honour the historical and unmarked graves surrounding the current cemetery boundaries.

This project will create an inventory of potential cultural heritage sites that may be impacted by climate change and assist the nation in developing local solutions. The project will build upon our oral history and knowledge base with new Elder and Knowledge Keeper interviews. The information will form the basis for the creation of the kʷikʷəƛ̓əm Place Names and Cultural Heritage Site Map, which will eventually serve as an interactive tool where users can hear audio of our hən̓q̓əmin̓əm̓ language from Kwikwetlem Elders, past and present;View historical photographs and see where they are located; and follow the map of the Kwikwetlem territory. A final aspect of the project is to move the sacred Xwti’tis Pitt River Transformer Stone from a residential property to IR1.

This X̱aad Kil / X̱aaydaa Kil language revitalization project combines language immersion with community engagement and language through culture.

The team will host three five day immersion camps throughout the year. They will revitalize language in the community by restoring intergenerational transmission through both institutional and family-oriented use of the Haida language. Each camp will focus on cultural activities such as storytelling, songs and land teachings.

They aim to keep the community engaged by offering a space to come together to share food and singing. In addition, they will share stories from participants on their experiences of immersion camps and language gatherings.

This project aims to re-explore the art of storytelling of ḵ’iigang (stories of supernatural beings) and gyaahláang (clan stories, historical stories) by developing a storybook that contains the tales of history, such as the great floods, Raven giving us tools to survive on the land, and others. Working with Elders and community members who have a wealth of knowledge in storytelling, we plan to hold two or three storytelling workshops this winter, as well as bi-weekly coffee meetings with community members and our storytellers. These workshops will also share information on digitization and transcription methodologies to provide our community members with skills and resources to produce material of their own in X̱aad Kil. The final product will be an illustrated book and audio resource including five stories in both English and X̱aad Kil.

Tsleil-Waututh Nation proposes the construction of a mortuary house structure to facilitate repatriation of ancestral Tsleil-Waututh human remains that have been previously exhumed from archaeological cemeteries at Tsleil-Waututh villages. Over 20 Tsleil-Waututh ancestors are currently in the possession of local universities and museums. Tsleil-Waututh would like to build a structure to house these ancestors so they can be returned home to be cared for in an appropriate manner, ensuring cultural safety and protection for these individuals.

With the help of a translator, these interviews were conducted in their Nedut'en language, then translated into English. The knowledge collected will be used in a teaching unit for students in the community.

properties.project_brief: Max will record the stories of an Elder/Knowledge Keeper who is 83 years of age and has an invisible disability (lifelong hearing loss). Collecting her stories and knowledge will preserve them for generations to come to teach them about courage, tenacity and perseverance in the face of difficult times, including daily life in a residential school and what it was like being separated from her family and community, and how they fit into contemporary life after residential school. One intention is to draw parallels of the difficulties of being separated from family because of residential schools to the contemporary experience of being separated due to the pandemic.

Oral histories will be recorded with a focus on stories that connect the community to cultural practices that support healing and wellness. This project will document two types of stories, including smaimai (true stories) about the Elders' childhood hardships, parental struggles, racism, loss of ancestral hunting and trapping trails and past sicknesses affecting their community. The other type of stories are captikʷɬ (creation stories), which hold lessons of hope and resilience that will help them heal from their grief and sadness. These stories are intended to be recorded and shared as a live-stream with their community.

One of our master basket weavers will teach the artistry of making our traditional baskets to a group of 10–15 participants. The program will include every part of the process, including harvest locations, place names in our language, what to take with you to harvest the roots, tools used to retract the roots and methods of cleaning, splitting and rolling up the roots on site. All parts of this process will be shared in our ucwalmicwts (language) and the program will incorporate flash cards from the Silent Speakers Program.

Tanya Lakes was an important gathering site along the Nuxálk-Dakelh Grease Trail and Salmon House Falls was a fishing site that historically brought together many groups. The sites hold burial grounds and remains of homesteads. This multi-faceted project mentors youth to learn traditional skills and knowledge, documents Elders’ observed changes to the areas and records Elders’ stories and memories related to family, culture  and history at the sites.

Ulkatcho territory has many traditional sites and trails that have not been formally mapped or recognized. Knowledge of their locations and history are at risk as Elders age and development increases. Ulkatcho First Nation will work to record Elders’ place-based oral histories and then pass them down through community land-based culture camps.

The Reclaiming My Language program is based on a successful course that has been developed by and for Indigenous Sami peoples. The course uses Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) to support Silent Speakers (people who know the language but do not use it) to overcome barriers to using their Indigenous language in their communities. The program will run for 10 weeks, from the week of October 2, 2022, to December 4, 2022.

Participants of ḵ̓a̱ngax̱ta̱we'gila (I will be making a button blanket) will learn how to create a button blanket. The program weaves together language, Kwakwa̱ka̱'wakw art and cultural heritage along with an intergenerational knowledge transfer.

properties.project_brief: We will start by bringing in a facilitator to teach the Gitmaxmak'ay Nisga'a Dancers & Society members the story behind Halayt dancing. We will then offer workshops on traditional medicines, making 1/2 masks and spinning wool for Cowichan-style hats and socks/slippers.

The Weaving in Sm'algyax Project consists of four weaving workshops that integrate learning language with learning cedar weaving to make berry baskets, cedar hats and Christmas decorations. Tsimshian artist Pearl Innis will mentor 10 students in each workshop, and fluent Sm'algyax speakers will teach Sm'algyax words and phrases related to the activities. The participants will learn traditional weaving, related language and the history of Gitxaala weaving.

This project, the construction of a community museum, is part of a larger infrastructure initiative to build a traditional Gitxaala longhouse and a cultural centre complex in the village of Lach Klan (Kitkatla, B.C.). This project will support the documentation of place names through field trips to key areas of Gitxaala Territory with fluent speakers, harvesters and youth. Further, it will work with fluent speakers and Elders to document Gitxaala adaawx (oral histories) and ayaawx (laws and protocols) and support the identification, digitization and archiving of important materials.

Finally, the project also aims to archive language and culture material and to build a user-centred, culturally informed content management system and facilitate appropriate long-term stewardship of language and culture materials in partnership with institutional repositories.

Haḥuułii is an organizing principal of Nuu-chah-nulth resource management for sustainability in a particular territory. Integration of language, traditional place names and ʕaḥuusʔatḥ ḥaḥuułi and its hereditary sytem and governance, which were spiritually gifted by Creator, is a central philosophy of ʕaḥuusʔatḥ ḥaḥuułism. Recognizing that Heiltsuk Bighouse has been such an important hub for cultural learning for our nation, we envision a restoration and enhancement project that will extend the lifespan of this beautiful building and create opportunities to train and mentor youth in new sectors of leadership, such as restoration and care for heritage spaces. In particular, we urgently need to address leaks in the traditional cedar-shake roof, and we need to repair the bleachers and drum log and other interior aspects that have been impacted by leaks.

Approximately 80 hours of legacy VHS recordings of Nuu-chah-nulth Tribal Council meetings, creating metadata of speeches in Nuu-chah-nulth language by past Elders, will be transcribed.

This Secwepemctsín language revitalization project combines language immersion and language documentation, recording and/or resource development. This Secwepemctsín language revitalization project combines language documentation, recording and resource development with community engagement and language through culture. The objective of this project is to build capacity to implement the strategic plan, allowing the Secwepemc Nation the opportunity to preserve and strengthen the language and nation as a whole. The team will collect and record the memoirs of Elders and Language Keepers; record and document Secwépemc language; and research documents, records, books and notes on the use and management of land and resources in pre-colonial eras. The project also includes engagement and storytelling sessions, a language summit to review their five-year plan and sharing resources through social media.

This Secwepemctsín language revitalization project combines language immersion and language documentation, recording and resource development with community engagement and language through culture. This project consists of advanced speakers/teachers-in-training being mentored by a fluent Elder twice a week in an immersion setting. Skills learned with the Elder will be applied to mini-immersion settings for new learners, which will accelerate their language learning/speaking abilities. Every mentoring session will be recorded for future use and phrases/words will be transcribed by a trained linguist. Secwepemctsín classes will be offered in person and online and language will supplement cultural activities such as on-the-land camps, plant harvesting excursions, drum making and songs and dances.

This Secwepemctsín language revitalization project combines language immersion and language documentation, recording and/or resource development with community engagement and language through culture. The team will develop learning materials for adult classes and language camps, as well as take- home kits for families. Their goal is to bring together the remaining fluent Elders to create and share strong learning resources for all Secwepemctsín communities.

This project consists of recorded weekly committee meetings of each language group in which participants share their language learning experience. The focus will be on protocol, storytelling and Indigenous reciprocity. These recordings will be shared on their website to stimulate Indigenous people to regain and validate their identity and Indigenous value systems.

In the Heart of Our Teachings, students will record Ucwalmicw teachings from our Elders. With those recording, students will then create an illustrated story book. We will also have our students paint a large mural of some of the teachings from a story an Elder has taught them. This way our Elders' stories will be available to the coming generations in book, digital and art format. Elders and students will also visit relevant areas in this territory so that these traditional places and traditional names will be preserved in the books and artwork created by the students.

Community members will be asked to bring all Ucwalmicwts language resources to community gatherings to start sharing and copying to create a Ucwalmicwts library.

The Nuxalk Ancestral Governance Project (NAGP) was initiated in 2015 to support self-determination and nation-led decision-making. This project will construct the Gitga’at Museum at MERRF. Because it will be a Class A Museum (bringing the total to 13 Class A museums in B.C.), the Gitga’at Museum will also offer exhibition space for members of the Tsimshian Group of Nations and other First Nations who lack suitable places for repatriating their artifacts. This project involves physical improvements to our cemetery infrastructure, which have gone virtually ignored under the mismanagement of the Indian Act. We intend to hire a community member to assist in implementing this sensitive project. Physical and infrastructure work identified in this project include the mapping of marked and unmarked graves in and around the Lakahahmen and Skweahm Cemeteries and associated data analysis; removal of vegetation; demolition of derelict structures; installation of a sheltered family gathering area with picnic tables; soil importation and grading; improved fencing; development and installation of signage; improved parking and walking trails; bringing water and electricity services to the cemetery site; addressing hazardous trees in and around the Lakahahmen Cemetery; and carving and raising a totem pole on site, carved from a cedar tree harvested from the cemetery, in accordance with Leq'a:mel tradition.

The Nisg̱a’a language class greatly benefits all the Nisg̱a’a Ts’amiks members who cannot return to their homeland to attend language classes or gain exposure through everyday life, feasts and ceremonies.

Tsleil-Waututh Nation proposes the construction of a mortuary house structure to facilitate repatriation of ancestral Tsleil-Waututh human remains that have been previously exhumed from archaeological cemeteries at Tsleil-Waututh villages. Colonization, development, associated archaeological work and looting have led to the disturbance, desecration and theft of Tsleil-Waututh ancestors buried at Tsleil-Waututh villages. Over 20 Tsleil-Waututh ancestors are currently in the possession of local universities and museums. Tsleil-Waututh would like to build a structure to house these ancestors so they can be returned home to be cared for in an appropriate manner, ensuring cultural safety and protection for these individuals.
